newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo must downgrade '97 economic targets - official.
newsitem.headline: Yugo must downgrade '97 economic targets - official.

text.p: Yugoslavia, still barred from major world financial organisations by an outer wall of sanctions, will have to downgrade its economic policy targets, the state news agency Tanjug reported on Friday.

"There is still an outer wall of sanctions, our hard currency assets have still not been released although we are entitled to them, we are still not members of the International Monetary Fund and World Trade Organisation," it quoted Yugoslav Economy Minister Rade Filipovic Filipovic as saying.
Industrial production is missing planned growth rates because business conditions at the beginning of the year have not changed much compared to 1996, Filipovic said.

According to official statistics, April industry output dropped 0.1 percent against March, but was 9.4 percent up on April 1996. Cumulative January-April industrial output was 7.3 percent up on the same period in 1996.
"The planned 1997 economic policy goals cannot be reached this way and with these dynamics," Filipovic said.
Lack of investments, shortage of working capital and insolvency inherited from 1996 were also blamed for the industry missing projected targets.

The government had predicted that in 1997 industrial growth would rise by 13.9 percent, agriculture by 6.0 percent and GDP by 13 percent. It also foresaw a 42 percent rise in exports and a 20 percent increase in imports.
Filipovic said the European Union trade benefits granted to Yugoslavia at the end of April came too late to improve results in the first half of 1997 and maybe even for the whole year.

The minister said tight monetary policy had produced excellent results in stabilising prices and the dinar exchange rate but that complaints from some businessmen that it was blocking economic activity should be looked into.
Inter-company debt has grown immensely and now exceeds cash in circulation, which is one of the reasons why business is blocked, Filipovic said.
The minister cautioned that participation of the grey economy in the overall economy was very high and consumer goods imports unrealistic and threatening domestic production.
